rows.title: Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB)
rows.originalText: The RYGB surgical review supplies operative anatomy and complication information but explicitly is not an anesthesia reference; anesthesia statements here rely mainly on broader bariatric guidance and general anesthesia standards.
rows.rationale: Surgical anatomy is distinguished from general bariatric anesthesia guidance; no RYGB-only protocol is claimed.

evidence.title: Procedure anatomy & case-specific priorities
bullets: The stomach is divided into a small proximal pouch and an excluded remnant. A gastrojejunal connection carries food into the Roux limb; a downstream small-bowel connection reunites food with biliopancreatic secretions.

The excluded stomach and bypassed proximal bowel are not accessed by ordinary passage from the mouth. Before any tube intervention or return to surgery, establish the patient’s actual reconstruction and the surgeon’s intended route.

Compared with sleeve or band, the reconstruction is more complex and has greater vitamin/mineral deficiency risk. Previous bypass patients may present with obstruction, dehydration or nutritional problems even after substantial weight loss.
In the 2024 MBSAQIP-based study reported by ASMBS in 2026, Roux-en-Y represented 32.82% of analyzed procedures. This dated study estimate should not be substituted for a local case mix.

evidence.title: PONV: prevention, rescue & surgical reassessment
bullets: Bariatric ERAS supports multimodal PONV prevention, reduction of perioperative opioid exposure and consideration of propofol-based TIVA when appropriate. This is bariatric guidance, not proof of one uniquely effective sleeve- or bypass-specific drug combination.

The guideline describes combining agents from three different antiemetic classes. Select the actual agents and timing for contraindications, interactions and patient risk; avoid duplicate dosing and account for sedation, QT risk and glycemic effects where relevant.

Document a rescue plan and reassess persistent vomiting, poor intake or vomiting accompanied by pain, tachycardia or systemic deterioration. Do not repeatedly treat nausea without considering a surgical complication.

evidence.title: Fluids, perfusion & venous thromboembolism
bullets: Aim for individualized euvolemia and adequate tissue perfusion. ERAS favors goal-directed fluid management where appropriate and avoidance of both excessive restriction and fluid overload.
Evaluate hypotension for anesthetic vasodilation, position/insufflation effects, bleeding and other causes. A fluid bolus is not the automatic answer to every reduction in blood pressure.

Use mechanical and pharmacologic VTE prevention according to bleeding risk, renal function, procedure and institutional policy. Prior VTE, immobility and other risk factors may influence extended prophylaxis; duration is individualized.

Plan early mobilization and postoperative hydration. Persistent tachycardia or dyspnea is not simply pain or dehydration until important causes such as bleeding, leak, respiratory compromise and VTE have been considered.

evidence.title: Analgesia, nausea prevention & recovery
bullets: Favor multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia. Local infiltration or regional techniques can reduce opioid needs; consider organ function, maximum doses and the procedure-specific surgical plan.

Use risk-based multimodal PONV prophylaxis and a rescue plan. Vomiting is particularly undesirable after upper-GI surgery and should not be dismissed when accompanied by pain, tachycardia or inability to tolerate intake.
NSAID suitability differs by procedure and patient. In Roux-en-Y patients, marginal-ulcer risk is a specific concern; do not automatically transfer a generic NSAID-based pathway to a bypass patient.
Resume oral intake and mobilization according to the bariatric pathway. Persistent intolerance, dehydration or nutritional problems need follow-up rather than repeated symptomatic treatment alone.

The ASMBS review identifies NSAID exposure as a marginal-ulcer risk factor after RYGB. A generic opioid-sparing NSAID pathway should therefore not be imported without an explicit bariatric-team assessment of alternatives and gastrointestinal, renal and bleeding risks.

ASMBS recommends postoperative PPI prophylaxis for at least three months after RYGB, with possible longer treatment for identified risks. Confirm the patient’s actual prescription and adherence; the review does not establish a universally safe NSAID dose or duration, and PPI therapy is not proof that NSAID exposure is risk-free.

evidence.title: NG/OG tubes, bougies & staple-line safety
bullets: Avoid routine or blind NG placement. Bariatric anatomy and fresh staple lines/anastomoses make uncoordinated tube placement hazardous; any necessary tube should be agreed with the surgeon and passed with careful technique.

If decompression is requested during primary surgery, an OG route may be used. BJA Education advises removing the decompression tube once the stomach is decompressed because an unintended tube can be trapped in a staple line.

Do not confuse an OG decompression tube with the calibration bougie intentionally used to size a sleeve. Confirm with the surgeon which device is present, its intended position and the timing of insertion, movement and removal before stapling.

Bougie passage and leak-test tube maneuvers carry perforation/injury risk. Do not force a device against resistance or undertake unfamiliar maneuvers without appropriate experienced assistance and surgical coordination.

Routine postoperative nasogastric decompression is not supported by ERAS. If postoperative decompression becomes necessary, review the exact reconstruction and arrange surgeon-directed placement rather than a blanket “never tube” or “routine blind tube” rule.

evidence.title: Intraoperative management & surgical coordination
bullets: Use secure weight-appropriate positioning with protection from sliding, pressure injury and nerve compression. Recheck access and airway security when the table is tilted or surgical access changes.

Maintain an individualized anesthetic with short-acting agents where appropriate, multimodal analgesia and planned PONV prevention. Avoid letting residual sedation, opioid accumulation or incomplete neuromuscular recovery become the limiting factor at emergence.

Use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and match blockade to surgical requirements. If deeper block is requested, plan reliable reversal and objective recovery rather than assuming elapsed time or apparent spontaneous breathing proves recovery.

Coordinate decompression, bougie placement, retraction, insufflation and any leak testing with the surgeon. Unexpected bleeding, airway-pressure changes or hemodynamic deterioration warrant reassessment rather than attribution to routine laparoscopy.

Monitor temperature and glycemia as indicated. Apply antimicrobial and thromboprophylaxis protocols matched to the patient and procedure; there is no single obesity dose rule that safely covers all medications.

bullets: Plan extubation as deliberately as induction. Use head-up positioning, adequate preoxygenation, awake airway control and objectively confirmed neuromuscular recovery; have equipment and assistance ready if re-intubation is necessary.

Continue prescribed home CPAP/BiPAP in the postoperative period when indicated. For increased desaturation risk, consider extubation directly to CPAP or HFNO; OHS or persistent hypoxemia may warrant bilevel/noninvasive ventilatory support and a higher-acuity setting.

Monitor for obstruction, hypoventilation, residual block and opioid-related respiratory depression. Supplemental oxygen can conceal impaired ventilation; a reassuring oxygen saturation alone does not exclude hypercapnia or ventilatory failure.

Choose PACU, monitored ward or higher-acuity care based on respiratory events, OSA/OHS, comorbidities, opioid needs and recovery, rather than BMI alone. Continue head-up recovery, mobilization and coordinated VTE prevention.

evidence.title: Airway difficulty, ramping & rapid desaturation
bullets: Anticipate difficult mask ventilation and upper-airway obstruction. Excess pharyngeal soft tissue, a large neck, reduced neck movement and loss of airway tone can compromise ventilation; BMI alone does not reliably predict difficult laryngoscopy.

Use ramped, head-up positioning as the default for bariatric airway management. SOBA recommends at least 30° head-up for preoxygenation where feasible; adapt to hemodynamic tolerance and positioning constraints rather than treating the angle as an absolute rule.

Start effective preoxygenation early with a tight mask seal. Consider positive-pressure support or CPAP when appropriate, and nasal oxygen/HFNO for peroxygenation; oxygen delivery during apnea does not replace ventilation when it is needed.

Reduced oxygen reserve and increased oxygen consumption shorten safe apnea time. Prepare adjuncts, two-person mask ventilation, rescue supraglottic airway, suction and an explicit failed-airway plan before induction.

Videolaryngoscopy is recommended first line by SOBA 2025. Choose a familiar blade and technique; maintain a low threshold to consider awake intubation when difficult ventilation/intubation or other airway risks are anticipated, not because of obesity alone.

A cuffed tracheal tube is the usual airway for laparoscopic bariatric surgery. Individualize rapid-sequence induction to aspiration risk while preserving oxygenation; a rescue device remains part of the plan even when not appropriate as the definitive airway.

evidence.title: Hemodynamics, pneumoperitoneum & monitoring
bullets: Obesity can be associated with increased blood volume/cardiac workload, hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction. OSA/OHS-related pulmonary hypertension and right-ventricular disease may make the patient less tolerant of hypoxemia, hypercarbia or major loading changes.

Pneumoperitoneum can increase vascular resistance/afterload and alter venous return; higher intra-abdominal pressure may reduce cardiac output. Reverse Trendelenburg and positive-pressure ventilation further change preload, so hypertension or hypotension must be interpreted in context.

Trend perfusion, blood pressure, rhythm, CO₂ and operative events, not a single number in isolation. Correct cuff sizing matters; select an arterial line for clinical indications rather than obesity alone.

Discuss insufflation and position changes with the surgeon. If cardiopulmonary tolerance is poor, reassess insufflation pressure, positioning, anesthetic effect and reversible causes rather than treating hypotension with fluid alone.

evidence.title: Preoperative assessment & obesity-related challenges
bullets: Risk is not defined by BMI alone. Review functional capacity, prior anesthetic and airway records, fat distribution, neck mobility, cardiopulmonary disease and the planned procedure or revision.

Screen for known or suspected obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS). Clarify home CPAP/BiPAP use, tolerance and settings; ask the patient to bring their device. Plan the recovery location before induction.

Assess hypertension, coronary disease, ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, diabetes, renal impairment and metabolic-associated liver disease. These comorbidities affect monitoring, fluids, drug titration and postoperative disposition.
Ask specifically about reflux, dysphagia, regurgitation, vomiting, gastroparesis, prior bariatric anatomy and GLP-1 therapy. A reported fasting interval alone does not settle aspiration risk.

Review oral intake, hydration, glycemia, anemia and nutritional concerns, especially after previous bypass or prolonged vomiting. Coordinate correction and perioperative medication plans rather than assuming all bariatric patients have identical requirements.

Confirm weight-rated table and transfer equipment, appropriately sized blood-pressure cuff, positioning aids, vascular-access plan and staffing. Consider ultrasound-guided access and invasive monitoring when clinical risk or unreliable noninvasive measurements warrant it.

evidence.title: GLP-1 medications & aspiration planning
bullets: Record the agent, indication, dose, last dose, recent dose increases and gastrointestinal symptoms. Escalation, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or other delayed-emptying conditions increase concern for retained gastric contents.

Most patients can continue GLP-1 therapy before elective surgery under multisociety guidance. Do not apply an automatic seven-day hold to every weekly formulation or cancel solely because a patient takes a GLP-1 drug.

For increased risk, coordinate a liquid-only diet for 24 hours, an individualized anesthetic/aspiration plan and, when appropriate and expertise is available, gastric ultrasound. Diet instructions must also respect the institution’s fasting policy.

Dose escalation or significant ongoing gastrointestinal symptoms may justify deferring elective surgery until risk improves. Make the decision with the surgeon, anesthesia clinician, prescriber and patient; account for glycemic consequences if treatment is withheld.

A medication history does not replace day-of-surgery assessment. If retained contents are suspected, weigh delay against proceeding with appropriate aspiration precautions; do not assume prolonged fasting guarantees an empty stomach.

rows.originalText: For bariatric surgery, use lung-protective tidal volumes of 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight (PBW). Optimal PEEP and the role of recruitment maneuvers remain uncertain.
rows.rationale: ERAS supports 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight. This is not actual-weight dosing or a universal PEEP target.

evidence.title: Pulmonary physiology & intraoperative ventilation
bullets: Obesity reduces functional residual capacity and expiratory reserve, limits chest-wall/diaphragm movement and increases oxygen demand. Supine positioning, induction and pneumoperitoneum compound these effects, promoting dependent atelectasis, ventilation–perfusion mismatch and rapid desaturation.

Set lung-protective tidal volume using height-derived predicted body weight, not actual body weight. ERAS describes approximately 6–8 mL/kg PBW as a starting range; titrate ventilation to the clinical situation rather than to excess adipose mass.

Individualize PEEP and recruitment to oxygenation, compliance/driving pressure and blood pressure. Do not use a mandatory PEEP of 10–15 cm H₂O for every patient; an oxygenation gain can be offset by hemodynamic compromise or overdistension.

Head-up/reverse Trendelenburg may improve respiratory mechanics. Pneumoperitoneum increases airway pressures and CO₂ load; trend end-tidal CO₂ and adjust minute ventilation, with blood gas assessment when clinically indicated.

New high airway pressure or hypoxemia requires assessment for reversible causes, including tube position/obstruction and mechanical problems; do not attribute every deterioration to body habitus. Interpret airway pressure alongside compliance, delivered volume and the operative events.

Minimize unnecessary circuit disconnection and loss of PEEP. OSA and especially OHS increase postoperative respiratory risk, so intraoperative ventilation and the extubation/monitoring plan should be linked.

evidence.title: Drug dosing: TBW, LBW, IBW & adjusted weight
bullets: TBW/actual body weight is the measured weight. LBW estimates non-adipose mass. IBW is a height-based reference weight; adjusted body weight combines IBW with a fraction of excess weight. These terms are not interchangeable, and an adjustment formula is drug- and protocol-specific.

Propofol induction: LBW is a commonly recommended initial scalar, with titration to loss of consciousness and hemodynamic response. A full TBW-derived bolus can be excessive; a scalar is a starting approach, not a guaranteed adequate induction dose.

Propofol maintenance/TIVA: do not copy the induction LBW rule into the infusion. Published approaches differ: older pharmacokinetic reviews discuss TBW/allometric clearance, while the BJA Education/SOBA chart uses adjusted weight. Use an appropriate obesity-validated dosing model or local TIVA protocol and titrate to effect; avoid uncritical linear TBW dosing.

Fentanyl and remifentanil: LBW-based initial dosing is supported in obesity reviews, followed by effect-guided titration. TBW-scaled remifentanil can produce excessive concentrations; opioid sensitivity, OSA/OHS and co-administered sedatives remain important.

Succinylcholine: TBW/actual weight is the commonly recommended obesity scalar when this agent is otherwise appropriate. This does not remove its usual contraindications or replace the institution’s dosing guidance.

Rocuronium: do not apply a single scalar to every context. SOBA 2025 uses LBW in its rapid-sequence example; older non-emergency dosing literature favors IBW to reduce prolonged block. Use the intended airway strategy and institutional protocol, then quantitative monitoring for subsequent dosing and recovery.

Vecuronium and atracurium/cisatracurium: IBW-based dosing is supported in the cited pharmacokinetic review to avoid unnecessarily prolonged block from TBW dosing. This evidence is older; confirm the current local drug protocol and titrate with quantitative neuromuscular monitoring.

Sugammadex: the March 2026 US BRIDION label specifies ACTUAL body weight, with dose selected by depth of block. Do not substitute IBW/adjusted-weight research regimens as the US-label default; severe renal impairment requires particular caution because use is not recommended by that label.

Acetaminophen, antibiotics, anticoagulants and local anesthetics each have agent-specific limits and obesity guidance. Do not extrapolate an opioid or induction scalar to these drugs or multiply adult maximum doses by TBW; use the current drug reference and institutional protocol.

evidence.title: Extubation, CPAP/BiPAP & postoperative monitoring
bullets: Plan extubation as deliberately as induction. Use head-up positioning, adequate preoxygenation, awake airway control and objectively confirmed neuromuscular recovery; have equipment and assistance ready if re-intubation is necessary.

Continue prescribed home CPAP/BiPAP in the postoperative period when indicated. For increased desaturation risk, consider extubation directly to CPAP or HFNO; OHS or persistent hypoxemia may warrant bilevel/noninvasive ventilatory support and a higher-acuity setting.

Choose PACU, monitored ward or higher-acuity care based on respiratory events, OSA/OHS, comorbidities, opioid needs and recovery, rather than BMI alone. Continue head-up recovery, mobilization and coordinated VTE prevention.

When a neuromuscular blocker has been given, confirm quantitative recovery at the adductor pollicis with a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9 before extubation. This does not mandate blockade in every case, and clinical strength or elapsed time alone does not prove recovery.

bullets: Anticipate difficult mask ventilation and upper-airway obstruction. Excess pharyngeal soft tissue, a large neck, reduced neck movement and loss of airway tone can compromise ventilation; BMI alone does not reliably predict difficult laryngoscopy.

evidence.title: Hemodynamics, pneumoperitoneum & monitoring
bullets: Obesity can be associated with increased blood volume/cardiac workload, hypertension, ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction. OSA/OHS-related pulmonary hypertension and right-ventricular disease may make the patient less tolerant of hypoxemia, hypercarbia or major loading changes.

Pneumoperitoneum can increase vascular resistance/afterload and alter venous return; higher intra-abdominal pressure may reduce cardiac output. Reverse Trendelenburg and positive-pressure ventilation further change preload, so hypertension or hypotension must be interpreted in context.

Trend perfusion, blood pressure, rhythm, CO₂ and operative events, not a single number in isolation. Correct cuff sizing matters; select an arterial line for clinical indications rather than obesity alone.

Discuss insufflation and position changes with the surgeon. If cardiopulmonary tolerance is poor, reassess insufflation pressure, positioning, anesthetic effect and reversible causes rather than treating hypotension with fluid alone.

evidence.title: NG/OG tubes, bougies & staple-line safety
bullets: Avoid routine or blind NG placement. Bariatric anatomy and fresh staple lines/anastomoses make uncoordinated tube placement hazardous; any necessary tube should be agreed with the surgeon and passed with careful technique.

If decompression is requested during primary surgery, an OG route may be used. BJA Education advises removing the decompression tube once the stomach is decompressed because an unintended tube can be trapped in a staple line.

Do not confuse an OG decompression tube with the calibration bougie intentionally used to size a sleeve. Confirm with the surgeon which device is present, its intended position and the timing of insertion, movement and removal before stapling.

Bougie passage and leak-test tube maneuvers carry perforation/injury risk. Do not force a device against resistance or undertake unfamiliar maneuvers without appropriate experienced assistance and surgical coordination.

Routine postoperative nasogastric decompression is not supported by ERAS. If postoperative decompression becomes necessary, review the exact reconstruction and arrange surgeon-directed placement rather than a blanket “never tube” or “routine blind tube” rule.

evidence.title: GLP-1 medications & aspiration planning

Most patients can continue GLP-1 therapy before elective surgery under multisociety guidance. Do not apply an automatic seven-day hold to every weekly formulation or cancel solely because a patient takes a GLP-1 drug.

For increased risk, coordinate a liquid-only diet for 24 hours, an individualized anesthetic/aspiration plan and, when appropriate and expertise is available, gastric ultrasound. Diet instructions must also respect the institution’s fasting policy.

Dose escalation or significant ongoing gastrointestinal symptoms may justify deferring elective surgery until risk improves. Make the decision with the surgeon, anesthesia clinician, prescriber and patient; account for glycemic consequences if treatment is withheld.

A medication history does not replace day-of-surgery assessment. If retained contents are suspected, weigh delay against proceeding with appropriate aspiration precautions; do not assume prolonged fasting guarantees an empty stomach.

evidence.title: Adult major burns: transfusion evidence & exceptions
bullets: The 2025 ABA blood-product guideline addresses hospitalized adults with acute burns; its restrictive RBC recommendation specifically concerns burns of at least 20% TBSA. The studied restrictive approach gives RBCs for a pretransfusion hemoglobin below 7 g/dL to maintain hemoglobin at least 7 g/dL, rather than maintaining at least 10 g/dL.

These thresholds do not apply to significant bleeding or hemodynamic instability in or outside the operating room. Active hemorrhage requires clinical resuscitation; do not wait for a laboratory threshold or delay source control.

rows.title: Escharotomy / Fasciotomy for Burns
rows.originalText: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as a source. The supplied procedure source supports local anesthetic infiltration of unburnt skin and optional sedation, but not the listed ketamine, propofol, fentanyl, or midazolam doses, ketamine infusion, or drug-specific plan.

evidence.title: Procedure-specific anesthesia priorities
bullets: Escharotomy releases constricting skin without intentionally opening the deep fascial compartments. Indications arise from evolving circulatory or respiratory compromise, not merely the visual presence of a burn.
Distal pulse loss is a late finding; surgical assessment integrates perfusion, Doppler and the clinical course. Ventilatory restriction may occur with significant chest or abdominal wall eschar.

Choose anesthesia and location to match urgency and physiologic stability, with airway/monitoring support immediately available. Reassess the result and arrange ongoing limb or respiratory surveillance.

Local anesthetic is needed for unburnt skin into which the release extends. Sedation may be used, and GA is not invariably required, but pain, associated injury, respiratory compromise and the ability to rescue the airway determine the actual plan; do not equate eschar with an entirely painless procedure.

Reassess distal perfusion or respiratory mechanics during and after release. Persistent compromise needs urgent surgical reassessment for incomplete release, a deep-compartment problem or another cause; neither a promised airway-pressure drop nor absent pulse is an adequate single decision rule.

evidence.title: Background, procedural, donor-site & neuropathic pain
bullets: Assess background pain, breakthrough pain, procedural pain and neuropathic symptoms separately. Include donor sites, positioning, lines and associated injuries rather than asking only about the burned wound.

Ketamine may support monitored procedural sedation or serve as an opioid-sparing adjunct. Appropriate staff, monitoring and airway rescue remain necessary; its use does not guarantee preserved ventilation or hemodynamic stability.

Dexmedetomidine may help with analgosedation, anxiety or withdrawal-related needs, but bradycardia and hypotension matter. Consider neuropathic agents for a suitable pain phenotype rather than adding them routinely to every burn case.

Regional techniques may improve donor-site or extremity analgesia and reduce opioid needs. Match the block to the operative sites and weigh infection, coagulation, anticoagulation, access and postoperative assessment needs; neuraxial techniques require particular caution in unstable or infected patients.

Plan pain control beyond the incision: dressing changes, mobilization and later procedures can be intensely painful. Include specialist pain care, anticipatory dosing and nonpharmacologic measures such as psychological support or distraction.

rows.originalText: The source supports usual timing within the first 48 hours after injury, but not a fixed 24–48-hour rule or timing independent of clinical assessment.

evidence.title: Procedure-specific anesthesia priorities
bullets: Escharotomy releases constricting skin without intentionally opening the deep fascial compartments. Indications arise from evolving circulatory or respiratory compromise, not merely the visual presence of a burn.
Distal pulse loss is a late finding; surgical assessment integrates perfusion, Doppler and the clinical course. Ventilatory restriction may occur with significant chest or abdominal wall eschar.

Choose anesthesia and location to match urgency and physiologic stability, with airway/monitoring support immediately available. Reassess the result and arrange ongoing limb or respiratory surveillance.

Local anesthetic is needed for unburnt skin into which the release extends. Sedation may be used, and GA is not invariably required, but pain, associated injury, respiratory compromise and the ability to rescue the airway determine the actual plan; do not equate eschar with an entirely painless procedure.

Reassess distal perfusion or respiratory mechanics during and after release. Persistent compromise needs urgent surgical reassessment for incomplete release, a deep-compartment problem or another cause; neither a promised airway-pressure drop nor absent pulse is an adequate single decision rule.

evidence.title: Excision blood loss & transfusion planning
bullets: Major excision can bleed rapidly from broad surfaces and donor sites. Bleeding may be underestimated because blood mixes with irrigation, collects beneath the patient or remains hidden under bulky dressings.

Estimate risk with the surgeon using the area and depth to be excised, infection, timing, donor sites and expected duration. Published percentage-of-blood-volume estimates vary and should not be treated as a reliable individual blood-loss calculator.

For substantial anticipated loss, establish suitable access, arrange crossmatched blood and a clear escalation/massive-transfusion plan; arterial monitoring and serial laboratory assessment may be appropriate.

Follow perfusion, serial hemoglobin, coagulation and temperature together. A stable-patient transfusion threshold is not a reason to wait during active major hemorrhage; follow the institution’s hemorrhage and blood-product pathway.

Tourniquets, staged excision, compression and topical/infiltrated hemostatic agents may limit bleeding. Coordinate agent identity, concentration, total amount and timing with the surgeon rather than assuming topical treatment has no systemic relevance.
Continue surveillance after dressings are applied and during transfer. Apparent completion of the procedure does not establish that wound bleeding has stopped.

evidence.title: Airway, inhalation injury & ventilation
bullets: Concerning findings include enclosed-space smoke exposure, facial/neck burns, soot, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridor, altered consciousness and respiratory distress. Facial burns or singed hair alone do not prove obstruction; assess the whole clinical picture.

Airway edema may progress over hours and worsen with resuscitation. Reassess frequently and secure a threatened airway before edema makes intubation difficult; urgency, oxygenation and anticipated difficult ventilation/intubation determine the approach.

Prepare advanced airway equipment and an explicit rescue plan. Existing airway burns, tenuous tube fixation and repeated transfers increase the consequences of accidental extubation; protect and reassess the airway throughout positioning and transport.

Lower-airway injury may cause bronchospasm, secretions/casts, impaired clearance, atelectasis and evolving gas-exchange failure. A normal initial chest radiograph does not exclude inhalation injury; bronchoscopy may help assess injury within the burn-team pathway.

Continue individualized lung-protective ventilation and required PEEP. Hypermetabolism increases CO₂ production; preserve oxygenation and avoid derecruitment during ventilator changes rather than using fixed settings for every burn patient.

Late facial or neck contracture can markedly reduce mouth opening and neck extension. Review earlier airway records and consider an awake airway strategy when indicated; a previously easy acute-burn intubation does not guarantee an easy reconstructive airway.

evidence.title: Background, procedural, donor-site & neuropathic pain
bullets: Assess background pain, breakthrough pain, procedural pain and neuropathic symptoms separately. Include donor sites, positioning, lines and associated injuries rather than asking only about the burned wound.

Use multimodal therapy tailored to physiology: acetaminophen with attention to liver function/total daily exposure, titrated opioids and selected adjuncts. NSAID decisions require renal, bleeding and graft-related risk assessment with the surgical team.

Ketamine may support monitored procedural sedation or serve as an opioid-sparing adjunct. Appropriate staff, monitoring and airway rescue remain necessary; its use does not guarantee preserved ventilation or hemodynamic stability.

Dexmedetomidine may help with analgosedation, anxiety or withdrawal-related needs, but bradycardia and hypotension matter. Consider neuropathic agents for a suitable pain phenotype rather than adding them routinely to every burn case.

Regional techniques may improve donor-site or extremity analgesia and reduce opioid needs. Match the block to the operative sites and weigh infection, coagulation, anticoagulation, access and postoperative assessment needs; neuraxial techniques require particular caution in unstable or infected patients.

Plan pain control beyond the incision: dressing changes, mobilization and later procedures can be intensely painful. Include specialist pain care, anticipatory dosing and nonpharmacologic measures such as psychological support or distraction.

evidence.title: Extubation, recovery & postoperative disposition
bullets: Extubation depends on airway patency/edema, gas exchange, ventilation, neuromuscular recovery, hemodynamics, metabolic status and anticipated ongoing bleeding or repeat surgery. Finishing a brief procedure does not make an unstable burn patient ready for extubation.

Consider continued ventilation/ICU care when inhalation injury, unresolved shock, major blood loss, significant edema or other organ dysfunction persists. Stable limited procedures and healed reconstruction may have different recovery needs.
Protect the tube, maintain required PEEP, continue essential infusions and warming, and hand over blood loss, fluids/products, latest laboratory results and evolving airway concerns during transfer.

Postoperative surveillance includes hidden wound bleeding, temperature, graft/limb assessment, renal/electrolyte trends and adequate analgesia. Coordinate pain and sedation plans with respiratory safety and rehabilitation needs.

rows.title: Abdominoperineal Resection (APR)
rows.originalText: Base44 is unverified and was not treated as an evidence source. Its fixed crystalloid volume, routine CVP and arterial-line claims, cell-saver and TXA use, epidural/TAP selection, and named induction or maintenance drugs are not established as APR-wide practice by the supplied sources.
rows.rationale: Fixed fluid/CVP, mandatory lines, cell salvage, TXA and epidural-drug recipes are not imposed.

evidence.title: Perfusion, fluids & blood loss
bullets: Aim for adequate perfusion without either fluid overload or undue restriction. Balanced chloride-restricted crystalloid is generally preferred for elective maintenance and boluses; routine colloid use does not have a demonstrated benefit in the colorectal recovery guideline.

Differentiate volume depletion, anesthetic vasodilation, positional effects and bleeding before repeatedly giving fluid. Treat vasodilation appropriately when volume is adequate; avoid prolonged hypotension and tailor pressure goals to baseline and organ risk.

Use trends in pressure, clinical perfusion, losses and laboratory data rather than a single CVP or urine-output value as a direct volume measurement. High-risk patients or substantial losses may justify invasive monitoring and goal-directed assessment.
Plan access and blood availability for the surgical extent and patient reserve. Reoperative or deep pelvic dissection can bleed substantially despite a minimally invasive skin incision.

evidence.title: Multimodal analgesia & regional options
bullets: Establish opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia before induction when possible. Acetaminophen and an appropriate regional or local technique can reduce opioid exposure; tailor the plan to incision, renal/hepatic function, bleeding risk and chronic opioid use.

Thoracic epidural is an option for open colorectal surgery with an acute-pain service, but is not routinely recommended for laparoscopic resection. Hypotension, motor effects, urinary catheter needs and anticoagulation timing influence the choice.

Abdominal-wall blocks address somatic incision pain but do not reliably replace treatment of deep visceral or perineal pain. Match coverage to the actual incisions rather than offering the same block for every colorectal operation.

NSAID-associated anastomotic-leak signals are molecule/class dependent; diclofenac has the strongest signal in the guideline discussion. Do not label all NSAIDs either universally safe or universally prohibited: reconcile anastomotic, renal, bleeding and cardiovascular risks with the surgical pathway.

rows.title: Colectomy (Open / Laparoscopic / Robotic)
rows.originalText: The Base44 claim that mechanical bowel preparation is optional or varies by surgeon is not an adequate summary of the supplied current elective-surgery guideline: ASCRS/SAGES recommends mechanical preparation combined with preoperative oral antibiotics. The older 2012 review disagrees about routine mechanical preparation; this draft gives precedence to the newer procedure-specific guideline for elective resection.
rows.rationale: Current elective ASCRS/SAGES combined mechanical preparation and oral-antibiotic guidance replaces the older blanket no-preparation statement.

evidence.title: Preoperative reserve, bowel preparation & aspiration
bullets: Review functional reserve, cardiopulmonary disease, anemia, renal function, nutritional status and recent intake/losses. Bowel preparation, poor intake, vomiting and an existing ileostomy can produce clinically important depletion before an apparently elective operation.

For elective colorectal resection, the ASCRS/SAGES guideline typically recommends mechanical bowel preparation combined with oral antibiotics, not mechanical preparation alone. The surgical protocol and contraindications determine the actual regimen; do not extrapolate this to acute obstruction.

Clear liquids up to 2 hours before anesthesia belong to an appropriate elective fasting pathway, not to patients with obstruction, impaired emptying or other elevated aspiration risk. Carbohydrate-loading evidence in this guideline primarily concerns patients without diabetes; individualize rather than applying it automatically.

Confirm recent antithrombotic exposure and the postoperative thromboprophylaxis plan before choosing neuraxial analgesia. An elective enhanced-recovery pathway must be modified for sepsis, significant coagulopathy or hemodynamic instability.

rows.originalText: Removed unsupported Base44 claims that ETT is universally required for colectomy, robotic docking necessarily prevents the surgeon from reaching the patient, and all robotic cases require a particular airway or emergence plan. The generic laparoscopy/robotics review prefers ETT but does not establish a colectomy-specific mandate.
rows.rationale: Laparoscopic/robotic access and airway constraints are addressed without treating all colectomies identically.

evidence.title: Pneumoperitoneum, ventilation & robotic access
bullets: CO₂ insufflation and head-down positioning reduce respiratory compliance and functional residual capacity and can increase airway pressure, atelectasis and CO₂ absorption. Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted/ideal body weight, not actual weight in obesity, and individualize PEEP and respiratory rate.

Reassess tube depth and bilateral ventilation after positioning and insufflation. Cephalad diaphragmatic movement can promote endobronchial migration; rising pressure is not automatically bronchospasm.

Secure the airway, IV connections and monitoring before docking because access may become restricted. Agree on how the team will obtain emergency patient access and coordinate all subsequent table or patient movement with the surgical/robotic team.

Sudden bradycardia during insufflation can reflect vagal peritoneal stretch. Notify the surgeon, interrupt the provoking insufflation and support circulation while evaluating other causes; persistent instability requires more than treating the monitor number.

bullets: Assess ventilation, hemodynamics, temperature, pain and airway swelling before extubation, particularly after long Trendelenburg positioning. When a neuromuscular blocker was used, verify quantitative recovery at the adductor pollicis with a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9.

Routine nasogastric tubes are discouraged after uncomplicated elective colorectal surgery. This does not prohibit therapeutic decompression for obstruction, persistent gastric stasis or a specific surgical indication.

For suitable elective patients, offer early oral intake and progressive mobilization according to the recovery pathway; the guideline supports a regular diet within 24 hours. Hemodynamic instability, obstruction, ileus or a complication requires individualized reassessment rather than forcing the pathway.

Plan urinary catheter removal around the operation and retention risk. The guideline generally favors removal within 24 hours after colonic/upper rectal resection and 24–48 hours after mid/lower rectal resection; these are not automatic deadlines after complex pelvic dissection.

Reassess tube depth and bilateral ventilation after positioning and insufflation. Cephalad diaphragmatic movement can promote endobronchial migration; rising pressure is not automatically bronchospasm.

Secure the airway, IV connections and monitoring before docking because access may become restricted. Agree on how the team will obtain emergency patient access and coordinate all subsequent table or patient movement with the surgical/robotic team.

bullets: Assess ventilation, hemodynamics, temperature, pain and airway swelling before extubation, particularly after long Trendelenburg positioning. When a neuromuscular blocker was used, verify quantitative recovery at the adductor pollicis with a train-of-four ratio of at least 0.9.

Routine nasogastric tubes are discouraged after uncomplicated elective colorectal surgery. This does not prohibit therapeutic decompression for obstruction, persistent gastric stasis or a specific surgical indication.

For suitable elective patients, offer early oral intake and progressive mobilization according to the recovery pathway; the guideline supports a regular diet within 24 hours. Hemodynamic instability, obstruction, ileus or a complication requires individualized reassessment rather than forcing the pathway.

Plan urinary catheter removal around the operation and retention risk. The guideline generally favors removal within 24 hours after colonic/upper rectal resection and 24–48 hours after mid/lower rectal resection; these are not automatic deadlines after complex pelvic dissection.

evidence.title: Evidence scope & clinical review
bullets: Adult clinical review draft, not a patient-specific order set. Adapt management to the actual procedure, comorbidities, physiology and current institutional policies; specialist clinical review is required before release.

Elective colorectal ERAS recommendations, emergency-laparotomy guidance and hemorrhoid-specific analgesia recommendations have different populations. Older narrative reviews are used for selected physiology and workflow, not as authority for outdated fixed fluid, bowel-preparation or drug regimens.
